report:
Conclusion: your skepticism is justified. There is **no good evidence that capsaicin treats breast cancer in humans**. The positive findings are almost entirely **preclinical**: capsaicin can inhibit proliferation, block migration, induce cell-cycle arrest/apoptosis in breast-cancer cell lines, and shrink MDA-MB231 tumors in immunodeficient mice (https://www.nature.com/articles/onc2009335). But those models do not establish human benefit, and oral capsaicin pharmacokinetics differ sharply from cell-culture exposure (https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/spicy-peppers-breast-cancer/).

A broad systematic review of capsaicin and cancer describes many mechanisms and laboratory studies, but not proven human breast-cancer therapy (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/oncology/articles/10.3389/fonc.2022.908487/full). A 2023 review is explicit: “The clinical value of per os capsaicin to complement chemotherapy is still speculative,” while noting animal evidence that capsaicin-sensitive nerves may even influence metastasis (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10177684/).

Human capsaicin use around breast cancer is mainly **high-concentration patches for neuropathic pain after surgery or chemotherapy-induced neuropathy**, not anti-tumor treatment (https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6694/18/14/2355). So the accurate statement is: capsaicin is biologically active and under investigation, with some concerning signals; it is **not an established breast-cancer treatment**. Patients should not replace surgery, endocrine therapy, chemotherapy, radiation, or targeted therapy with capsaicin.
